title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
gist: A Sydney team led by surgeon Carlo Pulitano says its automated Extended Organ Perfusion System kept a human liver alive at body temperature for seven weeks (unpublished), far beyond the prior ~two-week Swiss record. The bigger signal is that long-duration machine perfusion is shifting from organ transport toward 'organ medicine' — organ repair, organ multiplication, human-organ drug testing and isolated gene therapy — with startups (Aeternum, Apersys, Bexorg, Altos Labs) and two new scientific societies forming around it, though the clinical purpose of multi-week perfusion is still questioned.

insights.claim: A team led by Carlo Pulitano at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and the University of Sydney claims to have kept a donated human liver alive at normothermic (~37 °C) conditions outside the body for seven weeks, with details still pending publication.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Unpublished but field-credible record; watch for peer-reviewed publication as the validation catalyst for long-duration perfusion plays.
insights.quote: Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks
insights.locator: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept

insights.claim: The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was a liver in Switzerland that lasted around two weeks, so the Sydney result is roughly a 3.5x extension.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Step-change in ex vivo organ duration suggests the technology frontier is moving fast, not incrementally.

insights.claim: Automation of the perfusion system was the key to the record: across 55 human livers perfused by the Sydney team, livers on the automated system had average survival tripled to about four weeks versus manually adjusted systems.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Closed-loop automation (pumps + sensors + control software) is the value driver in perfusion devices — favors players with control/sensing IP over simple pump hardware.
insights.locator: Pulitano says the key to breaking the record

insights.claim: Most transplant organs survive only a few hours on ice, but over the last decade surgeons have shifted to warm or cold perfusion systems, which can double the time an organ can be held before transplant.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Perfusion is already a mainstream, growing transplant-logistics market, not just a research curiosity.
insights.locator: Most organs destined for transplant survive

insights.claim: University of Oklahoma transplant doctor Paulo Martins says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though perfusion can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: High per-procedure cost plus ~50% penetration at an active center indicates sizable revenue pools for perfusion device and service vendors.
insights.locator: Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts

insights.claim: Perfused livers apparently begin to repair themselves after a day or so, which led a Swiss team in 2022 to transplant a damaged liver after three days on perfusion — the longest any internal organ had been outside the body before a successful transplant.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Organ 'repair on the machine' could expand the usable donor pool by rehabilitating marginal organs — the nearest-term commercial use case.
insights.locator: Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits

insights.claim: Pulitano's startup Aeternum Life Technologies will help with a planned Sydney trial transplanting low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days, while Apersys, led by CEO Waldemar Hoffmann, was formed to commercialize the Swiss perfusion technology.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Private startups are racing to commercialize multi-day liver perfusion; the Sydney four-day trial is a near-term clinical milestone to track.
insights.locator: Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies

insights.claim: Apersys CEO Waldemar Hoffmann says the field believes Pulitano's record is real but doubts any surgeon would need a liver kept alive for nearly two months, and it is unknown how healthy the organ was at the end.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Multi-week perfusion lacks a clear transplant use case; value depends on non-transplant applications materializing.
insights.quote: The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be

insights.claim: Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs by dividing a liver and letting the sections regrow on the machine, as split livers regrow to near full volume in about two months in living donation.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: If proven, ex vivo organ multiplication would directly attack organ scarcity — a long-dated, high-optionality bet.
insights.locator: For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion

insights.claim: Perfused whole human organs are emerging as drug-testing platforms: US company Bexorg reanimates human brains with perfusion pumps for about a day to study experimental drugs and wants to extend this to two weeks, and Pulitano has tried adding gene therapies to perfused livers.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Human-organ models could displace some animal testing in preclinical pharma — a services market adjacent to perfusion hardware.
insights.quote: It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset
insights.locator: Similar experiments can be done on livers

insights.claim: Patents filed by billionaire-backed longevity startup Altos Labs describe introducing reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body, and Altos scientists have speculated about temporarily disconnecting a failing organ in a patient onto a perfusion machine to apply powerful genetic treatments without exposing the rest of the body.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Perfusion as an isolated-organ delivery route could de-risk aggressive gene/reprogramming therapies — a link between longevity biotech and perfusion tech.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs

insights.claim: Two new scientific societies have formed around long-term organ life support: the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy founded by Paulo Martins, and a China-based society launched in August by doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University to advance 'organ medicine'.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
entities: International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy
First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University
insights.so_what: Institutionalization in both the West and China signals organ medicine is becoming a recognized field — and a potential US–China research race.
insights.quote: What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation
insights.locator: Doctors probing the limits of organ life support

top_entities: First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University
